cvEn:
Lea Sharshevski Lifshitz was 32 years old when she was killed during Haganah training. She was a graceful, upright and beautiful woman, with clear eyes and dark braids wound around her head.

Lea was born on the third night of Hanukkah, 27 Kislev 5672 (17 December 1911), in the moshava of Zikhron Ya'akov, the one that is remembered as Binyamina. Her father, Shmuel Sharshevski, one of the first children born in the place, worked the land he had received from his parents, Gershon and Michal, who had come in the First Aliyah and were among the founders of the moshava. Lea was the second of five daughters and one son born to Alta and Shmuel. From a young age she helped with every task at home and in the yard, and also in the dairy that her family had set up. Alongside all these duties, she did not neglect her schooling, in which she proved to be a good student and a devoted friend, loved by pupils and teachers alike. She joined the Scouts group founded in the moshava, and was connected to the Scouts Legion in Jerusalem, which later merged with the Hugim in Tel Aviv to establish the pioneering youth movement Machanot HaOlim. When she finished her studies in the moshava, Lea continued at the WIZO girls' school in Tel Aviv, where she received her first training in farming and home economics. Friends from those days describe her as having something of a princess about her: a combination of nobility of spirit, a sensitive conscience and warmth.

At that time she met Moshe Mossensohn, who was then studying at Mikveh Israel, and the two became a couple. After completing her studies, she spent a year at Kvutzat Gevah in the Jezreel Valley, and in the summer of 1931 she joined Moshe in the Hugim group that settled on the banks of Ein Harod. When the Machanot HaOlim work company in Ra'anana was established shortly afterwards, they moved there. On the eve of Yom Kippur 1932, Lea gave birth to her first child, Dvora. Lea held various key roles in the young kibbutz near the moshava: she was in charge of the supplies store, the clothing store and the children's house. At that time the couple parted ways. The mother and daughter stayed on the kibbutz in Ra'anana, while Moshe moved to Kibbutz Na'an. In 1937 Lea was sent to study at the ideological seminar of HaKibbutz HaMeuhad, which lasted five months, and afterwards she went with her daughter for a year of training at the older kibbutz of Ashdot Ya'akov. There she met the kibbutz member Yisrael Lifshitz, and together they returned to their kibbutz, which had settled on land in the Beit She'an Valley and founded Ma'oz Haim. Here Lea built her new home. But she did not shut herself away with her family; she continued her work and public activity. She was in charge of the children's clothing store, and with care and good taste she worked to vary and improve the children's clothing despite the limits of the budget. She also coordinated the education committee and, on several occasions, was a member of the kibbutz secretariat. She did not stop her public activity despite a difficult pregnancy and the call-up of her husband Yisrael Lifshitz, who was mobilized as a driver with the British Army in Syria. In Av 5702 (1942) Lea gave birth to twin sons, Nadav and Assaf. These were the years of the Second World War, and she was alone, without a woman with her, when the time came. Even afterwards, long weeks passed before he came home on a short leave, and he immediately returned beyond the country's borders. Despite the heavy load and the difficulty of caring for two babies, Lea continued to carry all her roles in the kibbutz. She demanded much of herself and of others, with a highly developed sense of responsibility and a firm stand on principles that seemed important to her. Her fellow kibbutz members remember her as upright and straight-stepping, and called her affectionately Lea'sh.

All those years she was an active member of the Haganah. It was the winter of early 1944. Lea knew a renewed joy of motherhood; the warmth of the family nest had been rebuilt. She was radiant and happy in her life, and hoped that with the approaching victory her husband would return. The twins had just begun to take their first steps and to speak, and the word "Ima" (Mother) sounded so sweet to her ears. She talked at length with her daughter about love and youth, and the two found in each other a renewed, more mature friendship. Then, on a sunny day at the beginning of Shevat, Lea went out for weapons training. She knelt on the ground as she had been instructed, holding a rounded tin disc. Facing her was a young woman who had aimed her rifle carefully at the hole in the rounded metal plate a few metres ahead. Lea wanted to learn to shoot well. The thought of the Holocaust in Europe, of the helpless Jews facing the blackened muzzles of firearms, sharpened her feeling that she had to train, because this was what the hour demanded. She aimed the rifle at the target so that its blackened muzzle would be exactly at the height of her eyes. Before going out to train she had met her daughter on the way. She was in a hurry. In the evening she would make it up to her; she would be back in the room with the twins, in their happy corner, away from the cold outside. She would learn to protect her children. Looking at her daughter lying in front of her, she saw the glint of her pupil through the hole. She aimed carefully and pressed the trigger. There was a crack of gunfire. The rifle, which had been aimed correctly, had been loaded by mistake, a fact that had not been discovered in the weapon check before the training. When the weapon was fired, the bullet struck Lea directly in the head and caused her death on 2 Shevat 5704 (27 January 1944), ten days after she had turned 32. The next day the skies were overcast, and rain fell as she was laid to rest in the cemetery of Kibbutz Ma'oz Haim. There she is visited by those who, despite all the long years that have passed, have not forgotten her: the sons, who came to know her only in her absence, the daughter, all the family members, and among them her eight grandchildren, who did not have the chance to know her. Yet that particular shade of her eyes still shines in their gaze, and the Sharshevski lineage that she bequeathed continues to live on in the generations that follow.

On 9 Shevat 5704 (3 February 1944), the kibbutz newsletter "LaHaverim" printed the poem by Yitzhak Kafkafi, "And So Perhaps She Thought in the Last Moment." Lea's eldest daughter, Dvora Omer (Mossensohn), who began writing for children in the 1950s, portrayed her mother's character in several of her books, above all in her story "Direct Hit."
